title: The Secret Garden
author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
ru: Одинокая избалованная девочка находит в старом поместье запертый сад — и вместе с ним дружбу, здоровье и радость жизни.

chapters.title: Chapter 1. Nobody Remembers Mary
chapters.text:
Mary Lennox was not a nice little girl, and she did not look nice either. She had a thin face, thin yellow hair and a cross, angry look. She was nine years old, and she lived in India.

Her mother was very beautiful and loved parties, and she did not want a child. So Mary lived with her Ayah, an Indian nurse, and the other servants. They gave her everything she wanted, because when Mary was angry, she screamed and hit them. So she grew up to be the most selfish little girl you could imagine.

One very hot morning, Mary woke up and knew that something was wrong. Her Ayah did not come.

“Where is my Ayah?” Mary shouted at the new servant. “Send her to me!”

But the woman just looked frightened and ran away.

That day a terrible illness called cholera came to the house, and people began to die. In all the noise and fear, nobody remembered the little girl in the nursery. Mary found some fruit and a half-empty glass of wine on a table, and she ate and drank. The wine made her so sleepy that she slept for hours.

When she woke up, the house was silent. Very, very silent.

A little snake moved across the floor, looked at her with eyes like jewels, and slid out under the door. Mary was not afraid of the snake. She was afraid of the silence.

Then she heard heavy boots. The door opened, and two English officers looked in.

“A child!” said one. “Alone, in a place like this!”

“I am Mary Lennox,” said Mary, and she stood up very straight. “I fell asleep, and nobody came. Why did nobody come?”

“Poor little thing,” said the young officer sadly. “There's nobody left to come.”

Her father and mother were dead. Her Ayah was dead too. The other servants were dead or gone.

Mary did not cry. She hardly knew her parents.

First she stayed with an English family. Their little boy, Basil, laughed at her and sang: “Mistress Mary, quite contrary, how does your garden grow?” A contrary child is a child who always says no. Soon all the children sang it, and Mary hated them.

Then they sent her to England, to her uncle, Mr Archibald Craven. His housekeeper, Mrs Medlock, met her in London.

“She's a plain little thing — not pretty at all,” Mrs Medlock said. It was true, and Mary knew it.

On the train to Yorkshire, Mrs Medlock told her about Misselthwaite Manor. It had nearly a hundred rooms, and most of them were locked.

“Your uncle has a crooked back, and he's a sad, strange man,” she said. “He won't want to see you. So don't go putting your nose into things.”

It was night when they got off the train. A carriage took them on and on through the dark, and outside the wind made a deep, wild sound.

“Is that the sea?” Mary asked.

“No,” said Mrs Medlock. “That's the moor. Miles and miles of wild land, with nothing on it but grass and sheep.”

At last the carriage stopped in front of a huge, dark house. Only one window had a light in it.

Mary looked up at the black walls, and for the first time in her life, she felt very small.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. Martha and the Locked Garden
chapters.text:
When Mary opened her eyes the next morning, a young servant was kneeling by the fire. She had round red cheeks and a friendly face.

Mary looked at her coldly. “Who are you?”

“I'm Martha,” said the girl with a big smile. “I'm going to look after you.”

“Then dress me,” said Mary.

Martha stopped and stared. “Can't you dress yourself?”

“No. In India, my Ayah dressed me.”

Martha laughed, but not unkindly. “It's time you learned. My little brothers and sisters dress themselves, and some of them are only four.”

Mary went red. In India, nobody laughed at her. But Martha talked and talked, and Mary, who did not want to listen, began to listen.

Martha's family lived in a little cottage on the moor. There were twelve children, and there was never enough food, but they were happy. “And then there's our Dickon,” said Martha. “He's twelve, and he's always out on the moor. The wild ponies follow him, and the birds sit on his hand.”

Mary never thought much about other people. But she wanted to see this Dickon.

After breakfast Martha said, “Go outside and play. There are lots of gardens. But one of them is locked, and nobody can go in.”

“Why?” asked Mary.

“It was Mrs Craven's garden. She loved it more than anything. One day she was sitting on the branch of an old tree, and the branch broke. She fell and was badly hurt, and the next day she died. After that, Mr Craven locked the door. He dug a hole and buried the key, and nobody knows where it is. That was ten years ago.”

A locked garden! For the first time since she arrived, Mary was interested in something.

She went outside. There were gardens everywhere, with high walls and green doors. In one of them an old man was digging. He looked at her and did not smile.

“There's a garden on the other side of that wall,” Mary said, pointing. “But there's no door.”

The old man, Ben Weatherstaff, did not answer. He whistled softly instead. A little brown bird with a bright red breast flew down from the wall and landed near his foot.

Ben's face became softer. “The robin. He's the only friend I've got.”

“I have no friends at all,” said Mary. “I never had any.”

Ben looked at her for a long moment. “Then we're a good pair,” he said. “We're both ugly, and we're both as sour as we look.”

Was she really as sour as this cross old man? It was an uncomfortable thought.

The robin hopped closer and looked at her with his round black eyes.

“He wants to be your friend,” said Ben.

Mary bent down. “Will you be my friend?” she asked the robin. Her voice was soft and kind, and that surprised her more than anything.

That night, the wind roared around the house. Then Mary heard something else. It was far away, somewhere in the dark corridors, and it was not the wind. It sounded like a child crying.

The next morning, she asked Martha about it. Martha's face went red.

“It was the wind,” she said quickly. “Only the wind.”

But Mary knew that it wasn't.

chapters.title: Chapter 3. The Key
chapters.text:
Every day Mary went outside, and every day the cold wind from the moor blew in her face. She ran along the paths to keep warm. Soon her cheeks were pink, and at dinner she was hungry. In India she was never hungry. Now she ate it all.

“The moor air is good for you,” said Martha happily. “Mother says a child should be outside all day.”

One evening Martha came back from a day at home with a present. It was a skipping rope with red and blue handles.

“Mother bought it for you,” she said. “She says it's the best toy in the world for a child.”

Mary turned it over in her hands. “What is it for?”

So Martha showed her. She jumped and counted, jumped and counted, all the way up to a hundred.

Mary tried. It was hard at first, but she did not want to stop. Then she thought of something. Martha's family was poor, and the rope cost money. Mary wanted to say thank you, but she did not know how. Nobody ever taught her. So she held out her hand, very stiffly, like a grown-up lady.

Martha laughed and shook it. “Eh, you're a funny one,” she said.

The next morning Mary skipped all the way to the long path by the ivy wall. There was the robin, standing on a little pile of fresh earth. The earth was soft and dark. Maybe a dog dug there in the night. The robin was looking for worms.

Then Mary saw something in the earth. It looked like a ring of old, rusty iron. She bent down and picked it up.

It was not a ring. It was a key — old and brown, with earth in it.

Mary's heart began to beat fast.

“Maybe it's the key to the garden,” she whispered.

She put it in her pocket. She did not tell anybody, not even Martha. All day she walked up and down by the wall and looked for a door. But there was only ivy — thick, dark green ivy, everywhere.

The next day the wind was strong. Mary was skipping along the path again when the robin flew onto the top of the wall and began to sing.

“You showed me the key,” Mary said to him. “Can you show me the door too?”

At that moment, a sudden wind came and lifted the long ivy from the wall. Under it, Mary saw something round. It was the handle of a door!

Her hands were shaking. She pushed the heavy ivy away. There it was: an old wooden door with a keyhole in it. She took the key out of her pocket and put it in the hole. It fitted. It was stiff, and she had to use both hands, but slowly it turned.

“Thank you,” she whispered to the robin. It was the first real thank-you of her life.

Mary looked up and down the path. Nobody was coming. She took a deep breath. Then she pushed the door, and it opened, very slowly.

She stepped through and shut the door behind her.

She was standing inside the secret garden.

chapters.title: Chapter 4. Inside the Garden
chapters.text:
It was the strangest, loveliest place in the world, Mary thought.

High walls stood all around it. Over the walls and the old trees there were climbing roses — hundreds of them. But they had no leaves and no flowers. Their long grey branches hung from tree to tree like thin curtains. Everything was grey and brown and very still.

“How quiet it is,” Mary whispered. “I'm the first person here for ten years.”

Was everything in the garden dead? She walked slowly along a path. Then she saw something on the ground: little sharp green points, coming up out of the black earth. There was one here, two there, more and more.

“They're alive!” she whispered. “It isn't all dead!”

She did not know much about gardens. But she could see that the long grass grew so thick around the little green points that they had no room to breathe. So she found a sharp stick and began to dig and pull. She worked and worked, and she made a little clear place around every green point.

She forgot the time. She forgot to be cross. When she looked up at last, the sun was high, and she was very late for lunch.

“I'll come back,” she told the garden. “I'll come back every day.”

Martha was delighted when she saw Mary's pink cheeks and bright eyes. Mary ate two plates of meat and potatoes, and then a pudding.

“Martha,” she said carefully, “if I had a little spade, I could dig. And if I had some seeds, I could make things grow.”

“That's a good idea!” said Martha. “There's a shop in the village with little garden tools, and packets of flower seeds too. Our Dickon knows all about gardens. I'll write to him. He can buy them and bring them to you.”

Mary had some money. Mrs Medlock gave her a little every week, and in this big quiet house there was nothing to spend it on. She gave it all to Martha, and Martha wrote the letter at the table, slowly and carefully, with her tongue between her teeth.

After that, Mary waited. Every morning she ran to her garden, opened the door with her key and shut it behind her. Every morning there were more green points under the trees. She cleared the grass around them, and she talked to the robin, and the robin talked back. Nobody knew where she went. It was her very own secret.

But she was a little afraid too. Soon Dickon was going to come. Did he know about the garden? Could he keep a secret? Or would he tell everybody, and then they would take her garden away?

One warm morning she was walking through the park when she heard a strange, low sound. It was like a whistle, or a little song. She turned the corner and stopped.

Under a tree sat a boy of about twelve. He was playing on a wooden pipe. He had a round, funny face, red cheeks and very blue eyes. And around him, sitting quite still and listening, were a brown squirrel, a beautiful bird with a long tail, and two rabbits.

Mary stood very still too. She knew at once who it was.

chapters.title: Chapter 5. Dickon
chapters.text:
The boy stopped playing and smiled at her. Then he stood up — very, very slowly.

“You have to move slowly,” he said quietly. “Fast movements frighten them.”

The squirrel ran up the tree, and the rabbits hopped away, but they did not look frightened.

“I'm Dickon,” said the boy. “And you're Miss Mary. I've got your things here.”

He had a little spade, a fork, and lots of packets of seeds. “These are poppies,” he said. “They're easy. You just put them in the ground, and they grow and grow.”

The robin came and sat on a branch next to them.

“He's a friend of yours,” said Dickon. “He's showing off for you.”

Mary looked at Dickon carefully. “Dickon, can you keep a secret? It's a big secret. If anybody finds out, I think I'll die.”

“I keep secrets all the time,” Dickon said. “If I told people about every bird's nest and every fox's hole, nothing on the moor would be safe.”

“I stole a garden,” said Mary quickly. “It isn't mine. It isn't anybody's. Nobody wants it, nobody looks after it, and nobody ever goes into it. Come and see.”

She took him to the ivy wall and opened the door. Dickon walked in and looked around for a long time.

“I never thought I'd see this place,” he said at last, very softly.

“Is it all dead?” asked Mary. “Are the roses dead?”

Dickon cut a grey branch with his knife. Inside, it was green.

“Not this one,” he said. “This one's wick. As wick as you or me.”

“Wick?”

“That's how we say it in Yorkshire. It means alive.”

“I'm glad it's wick!” said Mary. “I want them all to be wick!”

They worked together all morning. Dickon showed her how to cut the dead wood and dig round the roots. He laughed a lot, and soon Mary was laughing too.

“There'll be roses everywhere in the summer,” he said.

When Mary got back to the house, Martha was waiting. “Mr Craven's here, and he wants to see you!”

Mary's heart jumped. Mrs Medlock took her to a room where a man was sitting by the fire. He was not ugly, but his shoulders were crooked, and his face was very sad.

“Are you well?” he asked. “Do they look after you? What do you want? Toys? Books? Dolls?”

Mary's voice shook a little. “Could I have a bit of earth?”

Mr Craven stared at her. “A bit of earth?”

“To plant seeds in,” said Mary. “To make things grow and see them come alive.”

He covered his eyes with his hand. “I once knew someone who loved growing things,” he said. “When you see a bit of earth you want, take it, child, and make it come alive.”

The next day he went away on his travels again.

That night it rained hard, and Mary could not sleep. Then she heard it again — the crying. This time she took her candle and went out into the dark corridor. She followed the sound, round one corner, then another, until she came to a door with a light under it.

Somebody was crying behind that door. Mary pushed it open.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. The Boy in the Bed
chapters.text:
It was a big room with old, dark furniture and a fire. In a huge bed lay a boy. He had a thin white face and big grey eyes with thick black lashes. He was crying, but not sadly. He was crying crossly, like a tired, angry child.

Then he saw the candle and stopped. He stared at her.

“Who are you?” he whispered. “Are you a ghost?”

“No,” Mary whispered back. Her own voice sounded frightened. “Are you?”

“I'm Colin Craven.”

“I'm Mary Lennox. Mr Craven is my uncle.”

“He's my father,” said the boy.

“Your father!” said Mary. “Nobody told me he had a son!”

“Nobody's allowed to talk about me,” said Colin. “I'm always ill, so I have to lie in bed. My mother died when I was born, and my father doesn't like to look at me. I'm going to have a crooked back like him. And then I'm going to die.”

He said it almost proudly.

“Do you ever go out?” Mary asked.

“Never. People stare at me. I don't let anybody look at me.” He lifted his chin. “Everyone here has to do what I say. If they make me angry, I get ill. And then they're sorry.”

Mary looked at him. He talked exactly the way she talked in India. It was not a nice thing to hear.

But he was very interested in her. He asked her about India and the moor. Then he asked about the gardens.

“There's a garden that's locked,” he said. “The servants talk about it. I'm going to make them find the key and open the door. Then they can carry me there.”

“Oh, don't!” Mary cried. She was so frightened that she took his hand. “If you make them open it, it won't be a secret any more.”

“A secret?”

“Yes! If nobody knows, and we find the door ourselves, then it can be our secret garden. Just ours.”

Colin's eyes became bright. “I never had a secret,” he said slowly. “I'd like that.”

Then he showed her something. On the wall there was a silk curtain with a cord. He pulled the cord, and the curtain moved back. Behind it there was a picture of a pretty, laughing girl. She had grey eyes, exactly like his.

“That's my mother,” he said. “I keep her covered. She smiles too much, and I'm ill and miserable. And she's mine. I don't want everybody to see her.”

The next morning Mary told Martha everything, and Martha was terribly frightened. “You found him? Oh, Miss Mary, I'll lose my job!”

“No, you won't,” said Mary. “He was glad I came. He wants me to come every day.”

And so she did. She told Colin stories about India, and about Dickon and his animals, and they talked and talked. One afternoon they laughed so loudly that the nurse came running. She stood at the door with her mouth open. Master Colin, laughing!

Then came a bright week of spring. The sun shone, Dickon came every morning, and the garden began to wake up. One day Mary worked with Dickon from morning until evening, and she forgot all about Colin.

When she came in, Martha was waiting at the door. Her face was white.

“Oh, Miss Mary,” she whispered. “Master Colin's in a terrible temper. He was waiting for you all afternoon.”

chapters.title: Chapter 7. A Terrible Night
chapters.text:
Colin was lying in bed when Mary came in. He did not look at her.

“Why didn't you come?” he said. “You were with that boy. I won't let him come here if you go and play with him and leave me alone.”

Mary's face became hard. She could be just as cross as Colin.

“If you send Dickon away, I'll never come into this room again!” she said.

“You will, because I'll make you!”

“You can't make me talk. I'll sit here and look at the floor!”

“You're a selfish thing!” cried Colin.

“And what are you? You're the most selfish boy in the world!”

“I'm not as selfish as you, because I'm always ill. And I'm going to die!”

“I don't believe it!” said Mary. “You just say that so people will be sorry for you!”

She walked out and banged the door.

In the middle of the night, a terrible noise woke her. It was Colin. He was screaming and screaming, and his screams went all through the old house. People ran up and down the corridors, but nobody could stop him.

Mary put her hands over her ears. Then she jumped up, ran down the corridor and threw open his door.

“Stop it!” she shouted. “Stop it! I hate you! Everybody hates you! You'll scream yourself to death in a minute, and I wish you would!”

Colin stared at her. Nobody ever spoke to him like that. He stopped screaming, but he was still shaking.

“I can't stop!” he said. “I felt the lump — I felt it. I'm going to have a crooked back, and then I'll die!”

“You didn't feel a lump!” said Mary. “Turn over and let me see.”

The nurse helped him to turn over. Mary looked at his thin back as seriously as a doctor.

“There's not a single lump there,” she said at last. “There are only the lumps of your backbone, and you can feel them because you're thin. I've got the same lumps, and you'll never have a crooked back. So don't you ever say it again!”

Colin turned to the nurse. “Is that true?” he whispered. “Do you think I could live to grow up?”

“Yes,” said the nurse, “if you go out in the fresh air.”

Colin lay back and breathed out slowly. He held out his hand to Mary.

“I'm sorry,” he said. “Will you sit with me?”

Mary held his hand and told him about the garden in a soft, quiet voice — the grey roses, the green points in the black earth, the robin. Colin listened, and soon he was asleep.

In the morning, Mary told him the whole truth. “I found the door,” she said. “I go into the garden every day, with Dickon.”

“Oh, Mary!” Colin cried. “When can I see it?”

“Soon. But first, Dickon wants to come and meet you.”

That afternoon the door opened, and Dickon came in, smiling his wide smile. He had a little newborn lamb in his arms, a crow on his shoulder and a young fox at his feet. A squirrel looked out of his pocket.

Colin sat up and stared. For a long moment he could not say a word.

chapters.title: Chapter 8. Colin Sees the Garden
chapters.text:
A few days later the weather was warm enough, and Colin gave his orders like a young king. All the gardeners must stay away from the garden paths. Nobody must look. Then two men carried him downstairs and put him in his wheelchair, and Dickon pushed it out into the sunshine. Mary walked beside them.

“This is the place,” Mary whispered at last. She pulled back the ivy, opened the door, and Dickon pushed the chair inside.

Colin covered his eyes with his hands. When he took them away, he looked round and round.

The garden was not grey any more. Everything was green. There were green leaves on the walls and on the trees, and the roses were full of tiny new leaves. Flowers were everywhere — yellow, purple, white. Birds flew in and out of the trees, and the air smelled sweet and warm.

“I'll get well!” Colin cried. “Mary! Dickon! I'll get well! And I'll live forever and ever and ever!”

They stayed all afternoon. Dickon showed Colin the robin's nest, and Colin laughed and talked until his white face became pink.

Suddenly Colin stopped and pointed. “Who's that man?”

There was a face on top of the wall. It was old Ben Weatherstaff. He was standing on a ladder, and he looked very angry.

“How did you get in there?” he shouted at Mary. Then he saw the wheelchair, and his mouth fell open.

“Do you know who I am?” said Colin coldly.

Ben stared at him. “Yes,” he said, and his old voice shook. “You've got your mother's eyes. You're the poor boy who's ill. The one with the crooked back and the weak legs.”

Colin's face went red. He sat up very straight.

“I don't have a crooked back!” he shouted. “Dickon! Come here!”

Dickon was beside him in a moment. Colin threw the blanket off his legs. His legs were thin — very thin. He put his feet on the grass. He held Dickon's arm. And then, slowly, he stood up.

He stood as straight as an arrow, and he looked strangely tall.

“Look at me!” he shouted up at Ben. “Look at me — you!”

Ben Weatherstaff began to cry. Tears ran down his old face.

“They told lies about you!” he said. “You'll be a man yet. God bless you!”

“I'm your master when my father is away,” said Colin. “Come down and come in here. I want to talk to you.”

A few minutes later, Ben came in through the door. He looked around the garden, and his face was full of feeling.

“I used to come over that wall,” he said quietly. “Every year, until my knees got too stiff. Mrs Craven loved her roses. She once told me, 'Ben, if I'm ever ill or go away, you must look after my roses.' So I did.”

That afternoon, Colin planted a rose in the earth with his own hands. Mary held it, Dickon pushed the earth down, and Ben watched.

When the sun went down, Colin was still standing, holding Dickon's arm.

“I'm going to come here every day,” he said. “And one day, when I can walk and run, I'm going to walk into my father's room and say, 'Here I am. Look at me.'”

chapters.title: Chapter 9. Magic
chapters.text:
After that, the three children were in the garden every day. Colin grew stronger and stronger, and he had an idea about it.

“There's Magic in this garden,” he said one morning. “It makes the leaves and the flowers grow. It made Mary strong, and it's going to make me strong too. I'm going to do a scientific experiment.”

So every morning they sat under a tree in a circle — Mary, Dickon, Ben, Colin, and even the animals. Colin spoke slowly and seriously, like a priest in church.

“The sun is shining. That is the Magic. The flowers are growing. That is the Magic. The Magic is in me. The Magic is in me.”

Then he got up and walked. Every day he walked a little further. Dickon taught him exercises — arms up, arms down, breathe in, breathe out. Soon Colin could walk all the way round the garden without help.

But this was the most important secret of all. Colin wanted to tell his father himself.

So in the house, he still sat in his wheelchair and complained. That was difficult, because now he was always hungry.

“I mustn't eat too much,” he said sadly. “Or they'll know I'm well.”

Dickon's mother helped. Every morning Dickon brought a basket from the cottage on the moor. Inside there was fresh milk, warm bread and potatoes cooked in the fire. The children ate it all in the garden. Then at lunch, Colin sent his food back to the kitchen, almost untouched.

“He isn't eating,” said the nurse. “But look at him — his face is round, and his eyes are bright! I don't understand it.”

The doctor didn't understand it either. Mary and Colin laughed so hard about it that they had to hide their faces in the cushions.

Mary was changing too. Her thin yellow face was round and pink now. Her hair was thick, and her eyes were bright. Nobody could call her a plain little thing any more. And she was not contrary any more either.

One day Dickon's mother, Mrs Sowerby, came into the garden. She was a tall, kind woman with a warm smile. Colin walked to her across the grass, and she held his hands and looked at him for a long time.

“Bless you, child,” she said. “You're so like your mother. My heart jumped when I saw you.”

“Do you think my father will like me?” Colin asked.

“He will,” she said. “He must come home. He must come home to you.”

Colin looked at her. “I wish you were my mother,” he said shyly.

Mrs Sowerby put her arms around him and held him close, like one of her own children.

At that time, Mr Craven was far away in Italy. For ten years he travelled from place to place, but he could not leave his sadness behind. He saw the most beautiful places in the world, but he never really looked at them.

One night he fell asleep by a quiet blue lake. In his sleep, he heard a voice. It was sweet and clear and happy, and he knew it at once.

“Archie! Archie!” called his wife's voice.

“Where are you?” he answered in his dream.

“In the garden,” said the voice. “In the garden!”

chapters.title: Chapter 10. Coming Home
chapters.text:
Mr Craven woke up in the morning, and he could still hear the voice. “In the garden,” he said to himself. “But the door is locked, and the key is buried.”

That same morning, a letter came for him. It was from a woman he did not know: Susan Sowerby, Martha and Dickon's mother.

“Please, sir,” she wrote, “come home. I think you'll be glad if you come. And I think your lady would ask you to come, if she was here.”

Mr Craven read it twice. Then he packed his bags and started for England at once.

On the long journey, he thought about his son. For ten years he did not want to see the boy, because Colin had his mother's eyes, and it hurt to look at them. Now he felt ashamed. What kind of father was he?

When he arrived at Misselthwaite, Mrs Medlock ran to meet him.

“How is Master Colin?” he asked.

“Well, sir, he's — he's different,” said Mrs Medlock. “He's out in the garden.”

Mr Craven walked across the grass and along the path by the long ivy wall, slowly, as if he was in a dream. He came to the old door and stopped.

He could hear sounds behind the wall. Running feet. Children's voices, trying to be quiet. And laughter — wild, happy laughter that they could not stop.

What was happening? Was he dreaming again?

Suddenly the door flew open. A boy came running out at full speed — a tall, handsome boy with pink cheeks — and ran straight into his arms.

Mr Craven held him and looked down at his face. And he could not breathe. The boy had grey eyes with thick black lashes. They were his wife's eyes.

“Who —?” he began.

“Father,” said the boy, “I'm Colin. You can't believe it. I can hardly believe it myself. I beat Mary in a race! I'm going to be an athlete!”

“It was the garden that did it,” he went on, very fast. “And Mary, and Dickon, and the animals, and the Magic. Nobody knows. We kept it a secret so I could tell you myself. Aren't you glad, Father? I'm going to live forever and ever!”

Mr Craven could not speak. He put his arms around his son and held him tight, and his eyes filled with tears.

“Take me into the garden, my boy,” he said at last. “And tell me everything.”

So they took him in. The roses were in flower everywhere — red and white and pink. Mary was there with her bright eyes and pink cheeks, and Dickon was there with his animals. They sat under the trees, and the children told him the whole story — the key, the robin, the terrible night, the Magic. Mr Craven laughed until he cried, and then he laughed again.

Later that afternoon, the servants looked out of the windows, and they could not believe their eyes. Mr Craven was walking across the grass towards the house, and he looked happier than anyone could remember.

And next to him, with his head up and his eyes full of laughter, walked Master Colin — as strongly and as steadily as any boy in Yorkshire.
